V01-A-001: Suppose a popular school has one remaining place and two applicants whose claims to it are, by every relevant measure, exactly equal. Giving the place to either child on the strength of some further feature, such as which parent argued more forcefully, would reward something that has no bearing on the claim. A lottery avoids this, because it gives each applicant the same chance and lets no irrelevant feature decide. Its fairness, in other words, lies not in the outcome, which still disappoints one family, but in the way the outcome was reached.
V01-A-002: Consent is usually treated as a switch: either a person agreed to something or they did not. Yet an agreement given under heavy pressure, by a worker who will lose her job if she refuses extra hours, hardly carries the same moral weight as one freely offered. The difference lies not in the words spoken, which may be identical, but in the options the person had when speaking them. Where those options are bad enough, where refusing would cost her something she cannot afford to lose, her 'yes' tells us more about her circumstances than about her wishes. Consent is therefore better understood as a matter of degree, its weight depending on how acceptable the alternatives to agreeing actually were.
V01-A-003: White lies are usually defended as small kindnesses: telling a friend that a mediocre meal was delicious spares feelings and seems to cost nothing. The cost, however, is hidden rather than absent, because it falls on the meaning of praise itself. If everyone knows that compliments are given regardless of merit, then a compliment can no longer tell anyone that their work was actually good. The friend who is always told that the meal was wonderful thus loses the one thing an honest friend could offer, which is a reason to believe it.
V01-A-004: Remove a single grain from a heap of sand and you still have a heap; no one seriously thinks that one grain could make that difference. Repeat the step patiently enough, though, and the same principle commits you to calling a lone grain, or even nothing at all, a heap. Something has to give, and the two obvious candidates each carry an unwelcome price. Denying the principle means insisting that somewhere there is an exact grain whose removal ends the heap, a boundary that no speaker could ever locate. Keeping it instead means conceding that words like 'heap', 'tall' and 'bald' cannot be trusted in strict reasoning at all, which asks far more of them than they were made for.
V01-A-005: Shoppers often say that they want as many options as possible, and shops compete with one another to provide them. Yet a page listing dozens of nearly identical phone plans can leave a customer more hesitant than a page listing only a handful. The reason is that each extra option adds to the effort of comparing, and raises the chance of later regret about the plans not chosen. More choice, in other words, is welcome only up to the point where that effort and that risk of regret begin to outweigh its rewards.
V01-A-006: People often come to like things simply because they have encountered them many times before. A song that seemed dull on first hearing, for example, can become a favourite after it has been played often enough on the radio. One explanation is that familiar things are easier to take in, and this ease is mistaken for a sign that the thing itself is good. Advertisers exploit exactly this confusion when they repeat a brand name far more often than any new information would require. Repetition of this kind persuades, if it does, not by argument but by making the product feel like something we already know.
V01-A-007: In a negotiation over price, the first number mentioned tends to pull the final agreement towards itself, even when it was chosen with little justification. Each side adjusts away from that opening figure as talks proceed, but adjustments of this kind are usually too small. Because the adjustment falls short, a seller who opens high can end up with a better price than one who opens with a reasonable figure and waits to be talked up. For a buyer facing such a seller, the lesson is to name a figure first, or else to refuse to treat the seller's opening as the starting point of discussion.
V01-A-008: On one influential view, an emotion is a kind of judgement: to be angry, for instance, is to judge that one has been wronged. The view neatly explains why anger usually fades once we learn that an apparent insult was an accident, since the judgement on which it rested has been withdrawn. It struggles, however, with the traveller who knows perfectly well that flying is safer than driving and is terrified on every flight all the same. If her fear were simply a judgement of danger, her knowledge should dissolve it, and its persistence suggests that emotions answer partly to something older and less easily corrected than belief.
V01-A-009: How long a pause in conversation can last before it feels awkward varies a great deal from one culture to another. In some places a silence of several seconds is a sign of respect, showing that the listener is giving thought to what was said. Elsewhere the same silence is read as disagreement or discomfort, and speakers hurry to fill it with words. When people from these two traditions talk, each may misjudge the other, one as evasive and the other as rash, without either intending any offence.
V01-A-010: When cheap paperback editions first became widely available, some critics warned that they would lower the standard of literature along with the price of books. Their fear was that publishers chasing mass sales would print mainly sensational fiction and crowd out serious work. What actually happened was more mixed: sensational fiction did multiply, but classics and serious essays also reached readers who had never been able to afford hardbound copies. The episode suggests that lowering the cost of access tends to enlarge every kind of reading at once, rather than simply replacing the better kind with the worse.
V01-A-011: Minority languages are lost far less often through outright prohibition than one might suppose. More commonly they fade within a few generations, as parents decide that their children's prospects lie in the language of schools and employers. Each such decision is reasonable on its own terms, which is precisely what makes the overall loss so hard to reverse. Campaigns that appeal only to heritage and pride ask families to set aside the very calculation that led them to switch in the first place. Efforts that last tend instead to give the language practical uses, in local media, administration or trade, so that speaking it no longer feels like a sacrifice.
V01-A-012: Many workplaces have abandoned titles and surnames, so that a junior clerk now addresses the managing director by her first name. The change is often celebrated as a flattening of hierarchy, a sign that everyone is now treated as an equal. Yet the director still decides who is promoted and who is let go, so the equality being celebrated extends only to the way people speak to one another. What has disappeared is the outward marker of rank rather than rank itself, which may make power harder to see and therefore harder to question.
V01-A-013: A gift appears to be the one transaction in which nothing at all is expected in return. Yet in many societies a gift that is never reciprocated slowly sours the relationship it was meant to strengthen. Oddly, repaying it at once, with something of exactly equal value, can give offence as well. An immediate and precise return turns the exchange into a purchase, cancelling the debt and with it the bond. What the gift creates, then, is neither a demand for payment nor a freedom from all obligation, but a lasting and slightly indefinite debt, and it is the indefiniteness that keeps the relationship alive.
V01-A-014: For a time, canals were the cheapest way of moving heavy goods such as coal and stone across parts of Europe. A single horse walking along the towpath could pull a barge carrying far more than any cart on the roads of the day. Once railways spread, however, they offered speed as well as capacity, and most canals steadily lost their traffic. Many of those that survive are now used mainly for leisure, a quiet afterlife for what was once vital industrial transport.
V01-A-015: Before printing, a single English word might be spelled in several ways, sometimes by the same scribe on the same page. Printing did not abolish this variety at once, since early printers sometimes adjusted spellings simply to fit a line of type. Over time, however, the repetition of the same forms across thousands of copies gave readers a sense that one spelling was correct. The standard that dictionaries later recorded was thus less a deliberate reform than the slow sediment of habits formed in the print shop.
V01-A-016: A government that wants to tax, conscript or feed its population must first know who that population is and where it lives. Early censuses were undertaken for exactly these purposes, and people often had good reason to fear the officials who came to count them. Their fear was well founded, since being counted made a household visible, and visibility was the precondition of being taxed or summoned. It is hardly surprising, then, that people wishing to stay beyond a state's reach have sometimes avoided being counted, giving false numbers or simply being away when the officials came. Such evasion, like the fear that prompted it, suggests that the census is less a neutral act of description than an instrument through which a state extends its reach.
V01-A-017: Complaints that manners, learning or public life have declined since some better age can be found in the writings of a great many periods. If each generation's complaint were accurate, the decline would have been continuous for thousands of years, leaving the present unimaginably worse than any past. Since that conclusion is absurd, the complaints are better read as evidence about those who make them than about the times they describe. What such evidence shows, most likely, is a habit of comparing an untidy present with a past known only through what was worth remembering, a contest the past always wins.
V01-A-018: Many prices in shops end in nine, so that an item is marked at 499 rupees rather than at a round 500. The difference of a single rupee is trivial, yet sellers persist with the practice in almost every kind of shop. One explanation is that shoppers read prices from left to right and give most weight to the first digit they see. A price beginning with four then feels distinctly cheaper than one beginning with five, even though the gap is almost nothing. Some upmarket shops deliberately avoid such endings for the same reason, preferring round figures that suggest quality rather than a bargain.
V01-A-019: Money already spent on a project cannot be recovered, whatever its managers decide to do about the project next. Logically, then, that spending should play no part in deciding whether the project ought to continue. In practice, managers often keep funding failing projects precisely because so much has already gone into them. Abandoning the project feels like admitting that the earlier spending was wasted, even though continuing only adds to the waste.
V01-A-020: Suppose one country can produce both machine parts and textiles with less labour than its neighbour needs for either. It might seem that such a country has nothing to gain from trade, since it can make everything more cheaply at home. But every hour spent on textiles is an hour not spent on machine parts, so what matters is which good each country gives up least to produce. If each specialises in the good it sacrifices least to make and trades for the other, both can end up with more of each than they could produce alone.
V01-A-021: In a large shopping centre, the department store at one end often pays far less rent for each square metre than the small boutiques along the corridors. This looks like favouritism until one asks why shoppers come to the centre at all. Many of them come for the large store, and on their way to it they pass, and sometimes enter, the smaller shops. The low rent is therefore a payment for a service, the traffic the large store brings to everyone else, which the landlord recovers through the higher rents of its neighbours.
V01-A-022: An antibiotic kills most of the bacteria it reaches, but a few may survive because of chance mutations that happen to protect them. These survivors then multiply with less competition, passing their protection on to their descendants. Every unnecessary course of treatment therefore gives resistant strains another opportunity to spread. It is this added opportunity that makes prescribing antibiotics for illnesses they cannot treat, such as common viral infections, not harmless caution but a real cost.
V01-A-023: A vaccine protects not only the person who receives it but also, indirectly, the people around them. When enough members of a community are immune, an infection that enters it finds too few susceptible hosts to keep spreading, and it dies out. Those who cannot be vaccinated, such as very young infants, are then shielded by the immunity of others. This shared protection, however, creates a temptation: each person may reason that, with everyone else immunised, their own vaccination adds little. If enough people act on that reasoning, immunity falls below the level at which it works, and the protection that made the reasoning plausible disappears.
V01-A-024: When it was first proposed, early in the twentieth century, that the continents had once been joined and had since drifted apart, most geologists rejected the idea. Their resistance is sometimes told as a story of closed minds, but they had a serious objection: no one could explain what force could move a continent. The fit of coastlines and the matching fossils on distant shores were suggestive, yet without a mechanism they could not overcome that objection. Only when studies of the ocean floor in the middle decades of the century revealed new crust forming at undersea ridges did the theory gain wide acceptance.
V01-A-025: Most people assume that if a medical test is highly accurate, a positive result from it must almost certainly be correct. Consider such a test, one that is right ninety-nine times in a hundred, used to screen for a condition that affects one person in ten thousand. Among every ten thousand people screened, about a hundred healthy ones will be wrongly flagged, against the single person who is actually ill. A positive result from such a test is therefore far more likely to be a false alarm than a diagnosis, which is why accuracy means little until we know how rare the condition is.
